A.explanation: Amplitude $3 \text{ V}$ is correct, but $125 \text{ Hz}$ uses a period of $8.0 \text{ ms}$ instead of the observed one full cycle width.

B.explanation: Peak height of 3 divisions at $1 \text{ V div}^{-1}$ gives $3 \text{ V}$, and a period of 2 divisions at $2.0 \text{ ms div}^{-1}$ gives $250 \text{ Hz}$.

C.explanation: Frequency $125 \text{ Hz}$ is too low by a factor of 2, and $6 \text{ V}$ is the peak-to-peak height, not the amplitude from equilibrium.

D.explanation: Frequency $250 \text{ Hz}$ is correct, but $6 \text{ V}$ counts from trough to peak instead of from the centre line to the peak.

hints: Count vertical divisions from the central horizontal line to a peak, then multiply by the y-gain of $1 \text{ V div}^{-1}$.
Measure one full cycle along the time axis in divisions - the distance between two adjacent peaks is about 2 divisions - then multiply by $2.0 \text{ ms div}^{-1}$ to get the period $T$.
Recall $f = 1/T$ with $T$ in seconds, and check whether you used amplitude or full peak-to-peak height for the voltage.
walkthrough: Read the CRO settings: y-gain $= 1 \text{ V div}^{-1}$ controls vertical voltage, time-base $= 2.0 \text{ ms div}^{-1}$ controls horizontal time.

Find amplitude: from the centre line to the top of a peak is 3 divisions, so $V_0 = 3 \times 1 \text{ V div}^{-1} = 3 \text{ V}$. The 6-division trough-to-peak distance is peak-to-peak voltage, not amplitude.
Find period: from one peak to the next peak is 2 horizontal divisions, so $T = 2 \times 2.0 \text{ ms div}^{-1} = 4.0 \text{ ms} = 4.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ s}$.
Combine $3 \text{ V}$ and $250 \text{ Hz}$. This is option B.
